name: New Zealand
covers: New Zealand's national sides (the All Blacks, Black Ferns and Black Caps) and Kiwi sport generally
dialect: New Zealand English, with everyday te reo Māori

words.means: Thanks, cheers, or 'awesome'. Short, warm and very Kiwi.
words.use: Chur for grabbing the tickets, bro.

words.means: Great, no worries. The 'as' just finishes it off; nothing comes after it.
words.use: Meet you outside the ground at six? Sweet as.

words.means: Totally. Strong agreement, or doing something flat out.
words.use: Best forward pack in the world? Hard out.

words.means: Broken or wrecked. Said of a bad injury, a car or a ruined pitch.
words.use: His knee's munted. He's gone for the season.

words.means: Hello, or thanks. Te reo Māori, used by everyone from broadcasters to the person next to you in the stand.
words.use: Kia ora, bro. You heading to the test?

words.means: Good, well done. Te reo Māori, heard at junior rugby and in the stands.
words.use: Ka pai, team. That's a proper first half.

words.means: Be strong, keep going. Te reo Māori, said to back a team before a big game or someone doing it tough.
words.use: Kia kaha, Black Caps. Big day tomorrow.

words.means: Prestige, authority and respect. Te reo Māori; people say the black jersey carries mana.
words.use: You don't just get handed that jersey. It's got mana.

words.means: Family, including the wider family and close friends. Te reo Māori; clubs and teams often call themselves a whānau.
words.use: The whole whānau's coming to the club final.

words.means: A Māori ceremonial dance performed at welcomes, celebrations and big occasions. The All Blacks perform one before tests, usually Ka Mate or Kapa o Pango, and fans treat it with respect.
words.use: Great seats for the haka. Goosebumps every time.

words.means: The Ranfurly Shield, the domestic rugby challenge trophy. The holder defends it at home and can lose it in any one game.
words.use: Shield challenge on Saturday. Let's bring the Log o' Wood home.

words.means: Wellington's main stadium (Hnry Stadium since March 2026), named for its round, metal look.
words.use: Freezing at the Cake Tin last night. That wind never stopped.

pronounce.why: Said the te reo way, three short sounds. 'MAY-or-ee' sounds out of touch.
Northland's city. The 'wh' is said like an f in most of the country.
Bay of Plenty city. No stress on the middle: not 'tor-RANG-ah'.
The province and its rugby side. Every vowel is an 'ah' or an 'ee'.
The best-known All Blacks haka, composed by the chief Te Rauparaha. Name it; don't attempt it.

lines.t: Eden Park's a fortress. Nobody beats us there.
lines.m: The All Blacks haven't lost a test at Eden Park since 1994.

lines.t: Bring on the Wallabies. That Bledisloe isn't going anywhere.
lines.m: New Zealand have held the Bledisloe Cup every year since 2003.

lines.t: Alarm's set for four. Test kicks off in Europe overnight.
lines.m: Tests in the northern hemisphere start in the early hours in New Zealand.

lines.t: Blowing a gale at the Cake Tin again.
lines.m: The Wellington wind is the standard moan about any game there.

lines.t: Small country, punching above its weight as usual.
lines.m: Kiwi pride, for the Black Caps especially; they won the first World Test Championship in 2021.

avoid.instead: the All Blacks, or the ABs
avoid.why: The Kiwis are the rugby league side. The rugby union team is the All Blacks.
Haka are performed at all kinds of occasions, not only as a challenge.
Mangling Māori is the fastest way to sound like a tourist.
Lumping New Zealanders in with Aussies goes down badly, especially in a Bledisloe week.

habits: Big tests are a social event: the pub, the club rooms or a mate's lounge, often with a barbecue first.
Tests played up north kick off in the early hours in New Zealand, so fans set alarms or stay up.
Saturday club rugby runs through every town, from juniors in the morning to the premier grade in the afternoon.
Fans wear black for the national sides: the All Blacks, the Black Ferns and the Black Caps.
unsure: words: 'tu meke' (awesome) and 'ka mau te wehi' left out: Te Aka has 'tumeke' only as 'startled', and no second source for the slang sense could be checked.
words: 'sweet as', 'hard out' and 'munted' are confirmed in Wikipedia and Wiktionary, but no New Zealand newspaper page could be opened to check them (web search was unavailable).
pronounce: Tauranga's te reo vowel is closer to [aʉ] than [aʊ]; the respelling is an approximation.

name: Australia
covers: Australia's national sides (the Wallabies and the cricket teams) and Aussie sport generally

words.means: Football, but which code depends on the city: Aussie rules (AFL) in Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth, rugby league in Sydney and Brisbane. Never soccer.
words.use: You going to the footy Saturday?

words.means: Afternoon.
words.use: Footy's on Saturday arvo, then a barbie at ours.

words.means: To support a team. Australians barrack for a club; they don't root for one.
words.use: Who do you barrack for?

words.means: A portable cool box, packed with drinks for the cricket or the beach.
words.use: Chuck a few more in the esky. Long day at the cricket.

words.means: A small bottle of beer, usually 375 ml.
words.use: Grab us a stubby while you're up.

words.means: Trash talk from fielders aimed at the batter. Aussie sides are famous for it.
words.use: Bit of sledging out there today. The umpires had a word.

words.means: Excellent. 'You little ripper!' when something great happens.
words.use: What a ripper of a catch!

words.means: The Melbourne Cricket Ground (the MCG), home of the Boxing Day Test and the AFL Grand Final.
words.use: Ninety thousand at the G. Unreal.

words.means: The last game of the season, which decides the premiership. AFL and NRL both have one.
words.use: Grand final week. Nobody at work's getting anything done.

words.means: A round of drinks. 'My shout' means I'm buying.
words.use: Your shout, mate. I got the last one.

words.means: A work or family competition to pick the winner of every game each week.
words.use: Dead last in the footy tipping again.

pronounce.why: Two syllables, the second one swallowed. Not 'mel-BORN'.
A z sound and a swallowed ending. Not 'BRIS-bane'.
The capital. Locals squash it to two syllables.
Far north Queensland city. No r and no i sound.
The Brisbane suburb that gives the Gabba its name. Everyone just says 'the Gabba'.

lines.t: Who do you barrack for?
lines.m: The first footy question you'll get. Answer with a club.

lines.t: Boxing Day at the G. Best day of the year.
lines.m: The Boxing Day Test starts at the MCG on 26 December.

lines.t: Blues or Maroons? You've got to pick a side for Origin.
lines.m: State of Origin rugby league: New South Wales (Blues) against Queensland (Maroons), three games every winter.

lines.t: One of these years we'll get the Bledisloe back.
lines.m: The Wallabies fan's hope. New Zealand have held it since 2003.

lines.t: Dead last in the tipping again. Don't ask.
lines.m: The office footy-tipping moan.

avoid.why: In Australia 'root' is slang for sex, so the question gets a laugh.
Canberra is the capital, whatever Sydney and Melbourne think.
In Sydney and Brisbane people say which code. Plain 'rugby' usually means union.
The full 'bourne' is the classic visitor's giveaway.

habits: Summer is cricket: the Boxing Day Test at the MCG on 26 December, then the New Year's Test at the SCG.
Grand final day means a barbecue and the telly. Victoria gets a public holiday on the Friday before the AFL decider.
State of Origin nights fill pubs in New South Wales and Queensland, everyone in sky blue or maroon.
Footy tipping competitions run all season at work and among mates.
unsure: words: 'Pom' left out: Wiktionary calls it mildly derogatory and sometimes an ethnic slur, and the ANDC says it can be friendly or derogatory.

words: 'shout' and 'grand final' are confirmed in Wiktionary and Wikipedia, but no Australian dictionary page for them could be opened; 'spewing', 'rapt' and 'dead set' were left out for lack of a second source.
habits: the Victorian public holiday before the AFL Grand Final and Origin's three-game format are from general knowledge; no page was opened to confirm them.

name: South Africa
covers: South Africa's national sides (the Springboks and the Proteas) and the URC sides: the Bulls, Lions, Sharks and Stormers
dialect: South African English, with Afrikaans and township slang

words.means: The Springboks. Afrikaans plural of 'Bok'; 'Go Bokke!' is the cry for any Springbok test.
words.use: Bokke! What a win.

words.means: Nice, great, tasty. The all-purpose word of approval, from Afrikaans.
words.use: Lekker win, hey. Proper Bok performance.

words.means: A barbecue over an open fire, and the gathering around it. Test day isn't complete without one.
words.use: Come round for the braai. Kickoff's at five.

words.means: Oh no, wow, or 'what can you do'. Covers frustration, surprise and resignation.
words.use: Eish, another yellow card. We're down to fourteen.

words.means: Hello, how are you? The everyday greeting.
words.use: Howzit, bru. You watching the game later?

words.means: Mate, buddy. Used to anyone, friend or stranger.
words.use: Relax, bru. There's still twenty minutes to go.

words.means: Brother, or a friendly 'mate'. From Afrikaans.
words.use: Thanks, boet. I owe you one for the tickets.

words.means: Hang in there, grit your teeth. Afrikaans, literally 'bite tight'; said when a team is defending for its life.
words.use: Ten minutes left and they're camped on our line. Vasbyt, boys.

words.means: Wow! or Oh no! An exclamation for anything shocking.
words.use: Jislaaik, did you see that tackle?

words.means: A party or a good time out.
words.use: If we win the final, it's going to be a massive jol.

words.means: A pickup truck. Fans braai off the back of one in the stadium car park.
words.use: We'll braai off the back of the bakkie at Loftus.

pronounce.why: The Bulls' ground in Pretoria. Afrikaans v is an f, and the d sounds like a t. Most people just say 'Loftus'.
Free State city, home of the Cheetahs. The 'oe' is an 'oo'. Locals often say 'Bloem'.
The university town near Cape Town. The 'sch' is just an s, not 'bosh'.
Stress on the last syllable, with a long 'ah'.

lines.t: Four World Cups, bru. Nobody's got more.
lines.m: The Springboks won in 1995, 2007, 2019 and 2023, more than any other country.

lines.t: Braai's going, Bokke at five. Lekker Saturday.
lines.m: Test day in a sentence.

lines.t: Bulls or Stormers? Can't sit on the fence for this one.
lines.m: Pretoria against Cape Town is the big domestic rivalry.

lines.t: Eish, that ref. Every week.
lines.m: The universal moan.

lines.t: The Proteas finally lifted one. Lord's, 2025.
lines.m: South Africa beat Australia in the 2025 World Test Championship final, ending a long wait for a major cricket title.

avoid.why: South African sides left Super Rugby in 2020 and now play in the United Rugby Championship.
It's a braai, over wood or charcoal, and the person at the fire is in charge.
The Proteas are the cricket team. The rugby side is the Springboks.
It's its own language, and plenty of fans' words come from it.

habits: Test days start with a braai, at home or in the stadium car park, with the fire lit well before kickoff.
Big games are watched at pubs, sports bars or a mate's place, with the whole family in green and gold.
Summer means cricket, and the New Year's Test at Newlands in Cape Town is a fixture on the calendar.
unsure: words: 'vasbyt' and 'jol' are confirmed in the Dictionary of South African English, but there was no Wiktionary page to cross-check 'vasbyt'.
pronounce: 'Loftus Versfeld' IPA follows Afrikaans spelling rules; no recorded pronunciation was found.
habits: braaiing in the car park at Loftus and the New Year's Test at Newlands are from general knowledge; no page was opened to confirm them.
words: 'shot' (thanks) and 'gees' (team spirit) left out; the DSAE has no entry for either.

name: Argentina
covers: Los Pumas and Argentine rugby, from the Buenos Aires clubs to Tucumán and Rosario

words.means: Come on, let's go! The basic cheer: '¡Vamos, Pumas!'
words.use: ¡Vamos, Pumas! One more scrum.

words.means: Grit, heart, fighting spirit. The quality Argentine fans prize most.
words.use: No stars today, just garra. That's Pumas rugby.

words.means: A devoted fan. 'Soy hincha de los Pumas': I'm a Pumas fan.
words.use: My dad's a real hincha. Hasn't missed a home test in years.

words.means: The crowd of fans, the support as a whole.
words.use: The hinchada was unreal tonight. You couldn't hear the ref.

words.means: Long live, up with. '¡Aguante los Pumas!' is pure Argentine fan talk.
words.use: ¡Aguante los Pumas! Win or lose.

words.means: The 'third half': after the game both teams share food and drinks at the club. As much a part of the day as the match.
words.use: Great game. See you at the tercer tiempo.

words.means: Hey, mate. The most Argentine word there is, used to get attention or between friends.
words.use: Che, did you see that try?

words.means: Go on! Or 'OK, sure'. Shouted at a runner in space, or used to agree to plans.
words.use: Dale, dale, he's through!

words.means: 'You'. Argentines say vos instead of tú, with their own verb endings ('vos sabés').
words.use: ¿Vos viste el partido? Did you see the game?

words.means: Kid, young lad. Said of a young player who's just broken through.
words.use: That pibe on the wing is only twenty and he's flying.

words.means: The Argentine barbecue, a long meal of grilled meat with friends and family.
words.use: Asado at the club, then we watch the Pumas.

words.means: The herbal tea drunk from a shared gourd through a metal straw. Not 'mate' as in friend.
words.use: Pass the mate, che. Second half's starting.

pronounce.why: The Spanish way, with an 'oo'. 'PYOO-muhz' is the English way.
Four clear syllables in the second word: not 'BWAY-nus AIR-eez'.
The rugby suburb north of the city, home of the big clubs CASI and SIC.
The northern province that breeds forwards. Stress on the last syllable.

lines.t: We've beaten the All Blacks now. Nobody laughs at us anymore.
lines.m: Argentina first beat New Zealand in 2020 and have done it again since.

lines.t: Beat the Lions in Dublin, che. Who saw that coming?
lines.m: Argentina beat the British & Irish Lions 28-24 in June 2025.

lines.t: Club rugby here is still amateur. That's the beauty of it.
lines.m: Argentina's domestic club rugby stayed amateur even after the national side turned professional.

lines.t: See you at the tercer tiempo.
lines.m: After the game it's food and drinks with the other team.

lines.t: Football's the religion, but rugby's the family.
lines.m: Rugby fans know football rules the country, and are proud of their own close-knit world.

avoid.why: Say it the Spanish way.
Argentines use vos, not tú, so textbook Spanish stands out.

avoid.instead: Rugby's huge in Buenos Aires, Tucumán and Rosario
avoid.why: The Pumas are a national team people adore, and club rugby has deep roots.

habits: Rugby is club life: families spend Saturdays at the club, juniors in the morning and the first team in the afternoon, then the tercer tiempo.
Big games go with an asado, a long barbecue with family and friends, and mate passed round the group.
Pumas tests in the Rugby Championship are watched together at the club, at home or in a bar.
unsure: words: most terms are confirmed in Wiktionary (with Rioplatense or Argentina labels) and Wikipedia, but Argentine dictionaries (RAE, ASALE) blocked automated access and no Argentine newspaper page could be opened to cross-check them.
words: 'la bajadita' (the San Isidro Club scrum technique) and 'bárbaro' (great) left out for lack of a checkable source.
habits: the club Saturday and asado habits are from general knowledge and the tercer tiempo sources.

name: Fiji
covers: Fiji's national sides (the Flying Fijians, the sevens teams) and the Fijian Drua

words.means: Hello! Literally 'life'. The everyday greeting, and a cheer.

words.means: Thank you; also 'good'.
words.use: Vinaka for saving me a seat.

words.tts: vee nah kah vah kah leh voo

words.use: Vinaka vakalevu, boys. What a tournament.

words.use: Moce, see you at the final.

words.means: Fiji, in Fijian. Before an i, the t sounds like 'ch'.
words.use: Go Viti! Toughest team in the Pacific.

words.means: Kava, the drink made from pepper-plant root, shared from a communal bowl at gatherings.
words.use: Bowl of yaqona and the sevens on the TV. Perfect Saturday.

words.means: Seven-a-side rugby, Fiji's great love. The men won Olympic gold in 2016 and 2020.
words.use: Everything stops when the sevens are on.

words.means: The war dance the Flying Fijians perform before tests, first taught to the team in 1939. A proud tradition, watched with respect.
words.use: The cibi before kickoff gave me chills.

words.means: A double-hulled canoe, and the name of Fiji's Super Rugby side, the Fijian Drua.
words.use: Drua at home this week. It'll be loud.

pronounce.why: The airport town. In Fijian, d has a soft n before it.
The capital, home of the national stadium.
The west's big town. The 'au' rhymes with 'now'.
The island off Viti Levu. In Fijian, q is 'ng-g' and b has an m before it.

lines.t: Bula! You watching the sevens?
lines.m: The greeting and the question that start most Fiji sports chats.

lines.t: Two Olympic golds. The whole country stopped.
lines.m: Fiji's men won sevens gold in 2016, the country's first Olympic medal, and again in 2020.

lines.t: Offload, offload! That's Fiji rugby.
lines.m: Fans love the running, offloading flair the islands are famous for.

lines.t: Drua at home this week. It'll be loud.
lines.m: The Fijian Drua play in Super Rugby, and home crowds are proud and noisy.

lines.t: Bowl of yaqona after the game?
lines.m: Sharing kava after a match is the Fijian way to wind down.

avoid.why: Fijian d has an n in front of it.
In Fijian, c is the 'th' in 'this' and b has an m before it.
The Flying Fijians reached the 2023 World Cup quarter-finals.

habits: Sevens tournaments bring the country to a standstill, with families gathered round the TV or the radio.
Kava (yaqona) is shared from one bowl at gatherings, and rugby is a favourite topic round it.
Rugby is the national sport; Saturday games draw whole villages and towns.
unsure: words: Fijian terms are confirmed in Wiktionary and Wikipedia only; Fiji Times, Fiji Village and FBC pages could not be searched or opened.
words: 'io' (yes), 'isa' and 'toso Fiji' left out for lack of a second source.
habits: the whole country stopping for the sevens is widely reported but no page was opened to confirm it.

name: Japan
covers: Japan's national side (the Brave Blossoms) and Japan Rugby League One

words.term: Buraiton no kiseki (ブライトンの奇跡)

lines.t: No side. Good game, both teams.

lines.t: 2019 was the best: first time in the quarter-finals.

lines.t: Off to Hanazono over New Year.

avoid.instead: Japan's played rugby for over a century

habits: The national high-school tournament at Hanazono, from late December to early January, is a winter ritual on TV and in the stands.
League One clubs are backed by big companies, and employees turn out to support their firm's side.
Fans wear the red-and-white hoops for the Brave Blossoms and applaud good rugby from both teams.
unsure: words: 'niwaka fan' (bandwagon fan) and 'jackal' (breakdown steal) were big 2019 rugby words but weren't in the buzzword top ten and no second source could be opened, so they're left out.
habits: applauding both teams is in keeping with the 'no side' spirit but no page describing crowd behaviour was opened.
words: 'oshi' comes from idol fandom; its use for rugby players is general fan usage, not a rugby-specific source.

name: India

words.use: What a finish, yaar!

lines.t: India-Pakistan? The whole country stops.
